post.yt_desc:
Your dollar was defined by a Spanish silver coin: the Coinage Act of 1792 defined the US dollar by the value of the Spanish milled dollar. This video follows silver from Potosí, in today's Bolivia, where the mita forced labor draft and enslaved Africans powered the mines and mint, to Ming China, where taxes were paid in silver and silver was worth about twice as much as in Spain in the 1590s. We cover the Manila galleons (1565-1815), Earl Hamilton's records of American treasure reaching Spain, a worked arbitrage example, and how the Spanish dollar left us the dollar sign, "two bits" and legal tender status until 1857. History and education only.

Flynn and Arturo Giráldez, Journal of World History (1995) and "Arbitrage, China, and World Trade in the Early Modern Period," JESHO (1995) and "China and the Spanish Empire" (1996); Ward Barrett, "World Bullion Flows, 1450-1800" (1990); Kris Lane, "Potosí: The Silver City That Changed the World" (2019); Encyclopedia of Latin American History and Culture, "Potosí"; GAO-05-535 (2005); The Art Newspaper (Aug. 26, 2026).
